entries.3832bc54298c37d958779a6286b47eed7f3b98ad: <div sID="gen14963" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Eccl.6" sID="Eccl.6"/> <div eID="gen14963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14964" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14965" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. The royal preacher goes on further to show the vanity of worldly wealth, when men place their happiness in it and are eager and inordinate in laying it up. Riches, in the hands of a man that is wise and generous, and good for something, but in the hands of a sordid, sneaking, covetous miser, they are good for nothing. 1. He takes an account of the possessions and enjoyments which such a man may have. He has wealth (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.2">ver. 2</reference>), he has children to inherit it (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.3">ver. 3</reference>), and lives long, <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.3">ver. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.6">6</reference>. 2. He describes his folly in not taking the comfort of it; he has no power to eat of it, lets strangers devour it, is never filled with good, and at last has no burial, <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.2-Eccl.6.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. 3. He condemns it as an evil, a common evil, vanity, and a disease, <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.1-Eccl.6.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. 4. He prefers the condition of a still-born child before the condition of such a one, <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.3">ver. 3</reference>. The still-born child's infelicity is only negative (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.4-Eccl.6.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>), but that of the covetous worldling is positive; he lives a great while to see himself miserable, <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.6">ver. 6</reference>. 5. He shows the vanity of riches as pertaining only to the body, and giving no satisfaction to the mind (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.7-Eccl.6.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>), and of those boundless desires with which covetous people vex themselves (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.9">ver. 9</reference>), which, if they be gratified ever so fully, leave a man but a man still, <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.10">ver. 10</reference>. II. He concludes this discourse of the vanity of the creature with this plain inference from the whole, That it is folly to think of making up a happiness for ourselves in the things of this world, <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.11-Eccl.6.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. Our satisfaction must be in another life, not in this.
entries.4a84a2be1d41f3c7310a5f35abb45405254ee2e5: <div eID="gen14965" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14964" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Miseries of Covetousness.</title> <div sID="gen14966" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it <hi type="italic">is</hi> common among men: <hi type="super">2</hi> A man to whom God hath given riches, wealth, and honour, so that he wanteth nothing for his soul of all that he desireth, yet God giveth him not power to eat thereof, but a stranger eateth it: this <hi type="italic">is</hi> vanity, and it <hi type="italic">is</hi> an evil disease. <hi type="super">3</hi> If a man beget a hundred <hi type="italic">children,</hi> and live many years, so that the days of his years be many, and his soul be not filled with good, and also <hi type="italic">that</hi> he have no burial; I say, <hi type="italic">that</hi> an untimely birth <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than he. <hi type="super">4</hi> For he cometh in with vanity, and departeth in darkness, and his name shall be covered with darkness. 5 Moreover he hath not seen the sun, nor known <hi type="italic">any thing:</hi> this hath more rest than the other. <hi type="super">6</hi> Yea, though he live a thousand years twice <hi type="italic">told,</hi> yet hath he seen no good: do not all go to one place? <div eID="gen14966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14967" type="x-p"/> Solomon had shown, in the close of the foregoing chapter, how good it is to make a comfortable use of the gifts of God's providence; now here he shows the evil of the contrary, having and not using, gathering to lay up for I know not what contingent emergencies to come, not to lay out on the most urgent occasions present. This <hi type="italic">is an evil which</hi> Solomon himself saw <hi type="italic">under the sun,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.1">v. 1</reference>. A great deal of evil there is <hi type="italic">under the sun.</hi> There is a world above the sun where there is no evil, yet God <hi type="italic">causes his sun to shine upon the evil</hi> as well as upon <hi type="italic">the good,</hi> which is an aggravation of the evil. God has lighted up a candle for his servants to work by, but they bury their talent as slothful and unprofitable, and so waste the light and are unworthy of it. Solomon, as a king, inspected the manners of his subjects, and took notice of this evil as a prejudice to the public, who are damaged not only by men's prodigality on the one hand, but by their penuriousness on the other. As it is with the blood in the natural body, so it is with the wealth of the body politic, if, instead of circulating, it stagnates, it will be of ill consequence. Solomon as a preacher observed the evils that were done that he might reprove them and warn people against them. This evil was, in his days, <hi type="italic">common,</hi> and yet then there was great plenty of silver and gold, which, one would think, should have made people less fond of riches; the times also were peaceable, nor was there any prospect of trouble, which to some is a temptation to hoard. But no providence will of itself, unless the grace of God work with it, cure the corrupt affection that is in the carnal mind to the world and the things of it; nay, when <hi type="italic">riches increase</hi> we are most apt to set our <hi type="italic">hearts upon them.</hi> Now concerning this miser observe, <div eID="gen14967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14968" type="x-p"/> I. The abundant reason he has to serve God with joyfulness and gladness of heart; how well God has done for him. <div eID="gen14968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14969" type="x-p"/> 1. He <hi type="italic">has given</hi> him <hi type="italic">riches, wealth, and honour,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.2">v. 2</reference>. Note, (1.) <hi type="italic">Riches</hi> and <hi type="italic">wealth</hi> commonly gain people <hi type="italic">honour</hi> among men. Though it be but an image, if it be a <hi type="italic">golden</hi> image, <hi type="italic">all people, nations, and languages,</hi> will <hi type="italic">fall down and worship it.</hi> (2.) <hi type="italic">Riches, wealth, and honour,</hi> are God's gifts, the gifts of his providence, and not given, as his rain and sunshine, alike to all, but to some, and not to others, as God sees fit. (3.) Yet they are given to many that do not make a good use of them, to many to whom God does not give wisdom and grace to take the comfort of them and serve God with them. The gifts of common providence are bestowed on many to whom are denied the gifts of a special grace, without which the gifts of providence often do more hurt than good. <div eID="gen14969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14970" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">He wants nothing for his soul of all that he desires.</hi> Providence has been so liberal to him that he has as much as <hi type="italic">heart could wish,</hi> and <hi type="italic">more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.7">Ps. lxxiii. 7</reference>. He does not desire grace for his soul, the better part; all he desires is enough to gratify the sensual appetite, and that he has; his <hi type="italic">belly</hi> is <hi type="italic">filled with</hi> these <hi type="italic">hidden treasures,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen14970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14971" type="x-p"/> 3. He is supposed to have a numerous family, to <hi type="italic">beget a hundred children,</hi> which are the stay and strength of his house and as a <hi type="italic">quiver full of arrows</hi> to him, which are the honour and credit of his house, and in whom he has the prospect of having his name built up and having all the immortality this world can give him. <hi type="italic">They are full of children</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>), while many of God's people are written childless and stripped of all. <div eID="gen14971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14972" type="x-p"/> 4. To complete his happiness, he is supposed to <hi type="italic">live many years,</hi> or rather many <hi type="italic">days,</hi> for our life is to be reckoned rather by days than years: <hi type="italic">The days of his years are many,</hi> and so healthful is his constitution, and so slowly does age creep upon him, that they are likely to be many more. Nay, he is supposed to <hi type="italic">live a thousand years</hi> (which no man, that we know of, ever did), nay, <hi type="italic">a thousand years twice told,</hi> a small part of which time, one would think, were enough to convince men, by their own experience, of the folly both of those that expect to find all good in worldly wealth, and of those that expect to find any good in it but in using it. <div eID="gen14972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14973" type="x-p"/> II. The little heart he has to use this which God gives him, for the ends and purposes for which it was given him. This is his fault and folly that he <hi type="italic">renders not again according to the benefit done unto him,</hi> and <hi type="italic">serves not the Lord God</hi> his benefactor, <hi type="italic">with joyfulness and gladness of heart, in the abundance of all things.</hi> In the day of prosperity he is not joyful. <hi type="italic">Tristis es, et felix?—Art thou happy, yet sad?</hi> See his folly: 1. He cannot find in his heart to take the comfort of what he has himself. He has meat before him; he has wherewith to maintain himself and his family comfortably, but he has <hi type="italic">not power to eat thereof.</hi> His sordid niggardly temper will not suffer him to lay it out, no, not upon himself, no, not upon that which is most necessary for himself. He has not power to reason himself out of this absurdity, to conquer his covetous humour. He is weak indeed, who has not power to use what God gives him, for <hi type="italic">God gives him not</hi> that <hi type="italic">power,</hi> but withholds it from him, to punish him for his other abuses of his wealth. Because he has not the will to serve God with it, God denies him the power to serve himself with it. 2. He suffers those to prey upon him that he is under no obligation to: <hi type="italic">A stranger eateth it.</hi> This is the common fate of misers; they will not trust their own children perhaps, but retainers and hangers-on, that have the art of wheedling, insinuate themselves into them, and find ways of devouring what they have, or getting it to be left to them by their wills. God orders it so that <hi type="italic">a stranger eats it. Strangers devour his strength,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.7.9">Hos. vii. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.5.10">Prov. v. 10</reference>. This may be well called <hi type="italic">vanity, and an evil disease.</hi> What we have we have in vain if we do not use it; and that temper of mind is certainly a most wretched distemper which keeps us from using it. Our worst diseases are those that arise from the corruption of our own hearts. 3. He deprives himself of the good that he might have had of his worldly possessions, not only forfeits it, but robs himself of it and throws it from him: <hi type="italic">His soul is not filled with good,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.3">v. 3</reference>. He is still unsatisfied and uneasy. His hands are filled with riches, his barns filled, and his bags filled, but <hi type="italic">his soul is not filled with good,</hi> no, not with that good, for it is still craving more. Nay (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">he has not seen good;</hi> he cannot so much as please his eye, for that is still looking further and looking with envy on those that have more. He has not even the sensible good of an estate. Though he looks not beyond the things that are seen, yet he looks not with any true pleasure even on them. 4. <hi type="italic">He has no burial,</hi> none agreeable to his rank, no decent burial, but <hi type="italic">the burial of an ass.</hi> Through the sordidness of his temper he will not allow himself a fashionable burial, but forbids it, or the strangers that have eaten him up leave him so poor, at last, that he has not wherewithal, or those to whom he leaves what he has have so little esteem for his memory, and are so greedy of what they are to have from him, that they will not be at the charges of burying him handsomely, which his own children, if he had left it to them, would not have grudged him. <div eID="gen14973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14974" type="x-p"/> III. The preference which the preacher gives to an untimely birth before him: <hi type="italic">An untimely birth,</hi> a child that is carried from the womb to the grave, <hi type="italic">is better than he.</hi> Better is the fruit that drops from the tree before it is ripe than that which is left to hang on till it is rotten. Job, in his passion, thinks the condition of <hi type="italic">an untimely birth</hi> better than his when he was in adversity (<reference osisRef="Job.3.16">Job iii. 16</reference>); but Solomon here pronounces it better than the condition of a worldling in his greatest prosperity, when the world smiles upon him. 1. He grants the condition of <hi type="italic">an untimely birth,</hi> upon many accounts, to be very sad (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.4-Eccl.6.5">v. 4, 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">He comes in with vanity</hi> (for, as to this world, he that is born and dies immediately was born in vain), and he <hi type="italic">departs in darkness;</hi> little or no notice is taken of him; being an abortive, he has no <hi type="italic">name,</hi> or, if he had, it would soon be forgotten and buried in oblivion; it would <hi type="italic">be covered with darkness,</hi> as the body is with the earth. Nay (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.5">v. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">he has not seen the sun,</hi> but from the darkness of the womb he is hurried immediately to that of the grave, and, which is worse than not being known to any, he has not <hi type="italic">known any thing,</hi> and therefore has come short of that which is the greatest pleasure and honour of man. Those that live in wilful ignorance, and know nothing to purpose, are no better than <hi type="italic">an untimely birth</hi> that <hi type="italic">has not seen the sun nor known any thing.</hi> 2. Yet he prefers it before that of a covetous miser. <hi type="italic">This</hi> untimely birth <hi type="italic">has more rest than the other,</hi> for <hi type="italic">this</hi> has some rest, but <hi type="italic">the other</hi> has none; <hi type="italic">this</hi> has no trouble and disquiet, but <hi type="italic">the other</hi> is in perpetual agitation, and has nothing but trouble, trouble of his own making. The shorter the life is the longer the rest; and the fewer the days, and the less we have to do with this troublesome world, the less trouble we know. <div eID="gen14974" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen14975"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14976"/>'Tis better die a child at four,<l eID="gen14976" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen14977"/>Than live, and die so at fourscore.<l eID="gen14977" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen14975"/> <div sID="gen14978" type="x-p"/> The reason he gives why <hi type="italic">this has more rest</hi> is because <hi type="italic">all go to one place</hi> to rest in, and this is sooner at his rest, <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.6">v. 6</reference>. He that <hi type="italic">lives a thousand years</hi> goes to the same place with the child that does not live an hour, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.20">ch. iii. 20</reference>. The grave is the place we shall all meet in. Whatever differences there may be in men's condition in this world, they must all die, are all under the same sentence, and, to outward appearance, their deaths are alike. The grave is to one, as well as another, a land of silence, of darkness, of separation from the living, and a sleeping-place. It is the common rendezvous of rich and poor, honourable and mean, learned and unlearned; the short-lived and long-lived meet in the grave, only one rides post thither, the other goes by a slower conveyance; the dust of both mingles, and lies undistinguished.
entries.f0e1e1dfc2d6fc836fa2c3872ac410a3b4e807ef: <div eID="gen14978" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Insatiableness of Desire.</title> <div sID="gen14979" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> All the labour of man <hi type="italic">is</hi> for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled. <hi type="super">8</hi> For what hath the wise more than the fool? what hath the poor, that knoweth to walk before the living? <hi type="super">9</hi> Better <hi type="italic">is</hi> the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire: this <hi type="italic">is</hi> also vanity and vexation of spirit. <hi type="super">10</hi> That which hath been is named already, and it is known that it <hi type="italic">is</hi> man: neither may he contend with him that is mightier than he. <div eID="gen14979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14980" type="x-p"/> The preacher here further shows the vanity and folly of heaping up worldly wealth and expecting happiness in it. <div eID="gen14980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14981" type="x-p"/> I. How much soever we toil about the world, and get out of it, we can have for ourselves no more than a maintenance (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">All the labour of man is for his mouth,</hi> which <hi type="italic">craves it of him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.26">Prov. xvi. 26</reference>); it is but <hi type="italic">food and raiment;</hi> what is more others have, not we; it is all <hi type="italic">for the mouth. Meats</hi> are but <hi type="italic">for the belly and the belly for meats;</hi> there is nothing for the head and heart, nothing to nourish or enrich the soul. A little will serve to sustain us comfortably and a great deal can do no more. <div eID="gen14981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14982" type="x-p"/> II. Those that have ever so much are still craving; let a man labour ever so much <hi type="italic">for his mouth, yet the appetite is not filled.</hi> 1. Natural desires are still returning, still pressing; a man may be feasted to-day and yet hungry to-morrow. 2. Worldly sinful desires are insatiable, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.10">ch. v. 10</reference>. Wealth to a worldling is like drink to one in a dropsy, which does but increase the thirst. Some read the whole verse thus: <hi type="italic">Though all a man's labour fall out to his own mind (ori ejus obveniat—so as to correspond with his views,</hi> Juv.), just as himself would have it, <hi type="italic">yet his desire is not satisfied,</hi> still he has a mind to something more. 3. The desires of the soul find nothing in the wealth of the world to give them any satisfaction. <hi type="italic">The soul is not filled,</hi> so the word is. When God <hi type="italic">gave</hi> Israel <hi type="italic">their request</hi> he <hi type="italic">sent leanness into their souls,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.106.15">Ps. cvi. 15</reference>. He was a fool who, when his barns were full, said, <hi type="italic">Soul, take thine ease.</hi> <div eID="gen14982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14983" type="x-p"/> III. A fool may have as much worldly wealth, and may enjoy as much of the pleasure of it, as a wise man; nay, and perhaps not be so sensible of the vexation of it: <hi type="italic">What has the wise more than the fool?</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.8">v. 8</reference>. Perhaps he has not so good an estate, so good a trade, nor such good preferment as the fool has. Nay, suppose them to be equal in their possessions, what can a wise man, a scholar, a wit, a politician, squeeze out of his estate more than needful supplies? and a half-witted man may do this. A fool can fare as well and relish it, can dress as well, and make as good a figure in any public appearance, as a wise man; so that if there were not pleasures and honour peculiar to the mind, which <hi type="italic">the wise man has more than the fool,</hi> as to this world they would be upon a level. <div eID="gen14983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14984" type="x-p"/> IV. Even a poor man, who has business, and is discreet, diligent, and dexterous, in the management of it, may get as comfortably through this world as he that is loaded with an overgrown estate. Consider <hi type="italic">what the poor has</hi> less than the rich, if he but <hi type="italic">knows to walk before the living,</hi> knows how to conduct himself decently, and do his duty to all, how to get an honest livelihood by his labour, how to spend his time well and improve his opportunities. <hi type="italic">What has</hi> he? Why, he is better beloved and more respected among his neighbours, and has a better interest than many a rich man that is griping and haughty. <hi type="italic">What has</hi> he? Why he has as much of the comfort of this life, has <hi type="italic">food and raiment,</hi> and is <hi type="italic">therewith content,</hi> and so is as truly rich as he that has abundance. <div eID="gen14984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14985" type="x-p"/> V. The enjoyment of what we have cannot but be acknowledged more rational than a greedy grasping at more (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Better is the sight of the eyes,</hi> making the best of that which is present, <hi type="italic">than the wandering of the desire,</hi> the uneasy walking of the soul after things at a distance, and the affecting of a variety of imaginary satisfactions. He is much happier that is always content, though he has ever so little, than he that is always coveting, though he has ever so much. We cannot say, <hi type="italic">Better is the sight of the eyes than the</hi> fixing <hi type="italic">of the desire</hi> upon God, and the resting of the soul in him; it is better to live by faith in things to come than to live by sense, which dwells only upon present things; but <hi type="italic">better is the sight of the eyes than the</hi> roving <hi type="italic">of the desire</hi> after the world, and the things of it, than which nothing is more uncertain nor more unsatisfying at the best. <hi type="italic">This wandering of the desire is vanity and vexation of spirit.</hi> It <hi type="italic">is vanity</hi> at the best; if what is desired, be obtained, it proves not what we promised ourselves from it, but commonly <hi type="italic">the wandering desire</hi> is crossed and disappointed, and then it turns to <hi type="italic">vexation of spirit.</hi> <div eID="gen14985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14986" type="x-p"/> VI. Our lot, whatever it is, is that which is appointed us by the counsel of God, which cannot be altered, and it is therefore our wisdom to reconcile ourselves to it and cheerfully to acquiesce in it (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">That which has been,</hi> or (as some read it) <hi type="italic">that which is,</hi> and so likewise that which shall be, <hi type="italic">is named already;</hi> it is already determined in the divine foreknowledge, and all our care and pains cannot make it otherwise than as it is fixed. <hi type="italic">Jacta est alea—The die is cast.</hi> It is therefore folly to quarrel with that which will be as it is, and wisdom to make a virtue of necessity. We shall have what pleases God, and let that please us. <div eID="gen14986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14987" type="x-p"/> VII. Whatever we attain to in this world, still we are but men, and the greatest possessions and preferments cannot set us above the common accidents of human life: <hi type="italic">That which has been,</hi> and is, that busy animal that makes such a stir and such a noise in the world, <hi type="italic">is named already.</hi> He that made him gave him his name, <hi type="italic">and it is known that it is man;</hi> that is his name by which he must know himself, and it is a humbling name, <reference osisRef="Gen.5.2">Gen. v. 2</reference>. He <hi type="italic">called their name Adam;</hi> and all theirs have the same character, <hi type="italic">red earth.</hi> Though a man could make himself master of all the treasures of kings and provinces, yet he is a man still, mean, mutable, and mortal, and may at any time be involved in the calamities that are <hi type="italic">common to men.</hi> It is good for rich and great men to know and consider that they are <hi type="italic">but men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.9.20">Ps. ix. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">It is known that</hi> they are but men; let them put what face they will upon it, and, like the king of Tyre, <hi type="italic">set their heart as the heart of God,</hi> yet the Egyptians are men, and not gods, and it is known that they are so. <div eID="gen14987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14988" type="x-p"/> VIII. How far soever our desires wander, and how closely soever our endeavours keep pace with them, we cannot strive with the divine Providence, but must submit to the disposals of it, whether we will or no. If <hi type="italic">it is man, he may not contend with him that is mightier than he.</hi> It is presumption to arraign God's proceedings, and to charge him with folly or iniquity; nor is it to any purpose to complain of him, for <hi type="italic">he is in one mind and who can turn him?</hi> Elihu pacifies Job with this incontest able principle, That <hi type="italic">God is greater than man</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.33.12">Job xxxiii. 12</reference>) and therefore <hi type="italic">man may not contend with him,</hi> nor resist his judgments, when they come with commission. A man cannot with the greatest riches make his part good against the arrests of sickness or death, but must yield to his fate.
entries.2f1184effceaf30534bbdeb7636beac8836763a4: <div eID="gen14988" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Insatiableness of Desire.</title> <div sID="gen14989" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Seeing there be many things that increase vanity, what <hi type="italic">is</hi> man the better? <hi type="super">12</hi> For who knoweth what <hi type="italic">is</hi> good for man in <hi type="italic">this</hi> life, all the days of his vain life which he spendeth as a shadow? for who can tell a man what shall be after him under the sun? <div eID="gen14989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14990" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. Solomon lays down his conclusion which he had undertaken to prove, as that which was fully confirmed by the foregoing discourse: <hi type="italic">There be many things that increase vanity;</hi> the life of man is vain, at the best, and there are abundance of accidents that concur to make it more so; even that which pretends to increase the vanity and make it more vexatious. 2. He draws some inferences from it, which serve further to evince the truth of it. (1.) That a man is never the nearer to true happiness for the abundance that he has in this world: <hi type="italic">What is man the better</hi> for his wealth and pleasure, his honour and preferment? What remains to man? What residuum has he, what overplus, what real advantage, when he comes to balance his accounts? Nothing that will do him any good or turn to account. (2.) That we do not know what to wish for, because that which we promise ourselves most satisfaction in often proves most vexatious to us: <hi type="italic">Who knows what is good for a man in this life,</hi> where every thing is vanity, and any thing, even that which we most covet, may prove a calamity to us? Thoughtful people are in care to do every thing for the best, if they knew it; but as it is an instance of the corruption of our hearts that we are apt to desire that as good for us which is really hurtful, as children that cry for knives to cut their fingers with, so is it an instance of the vanity of this world that what, according to all probable conjectures, seems to be for the best, often proves otherwise; such is our shortsightedness concerning the issues and events of things, and such broken reeds are all our creature-confidences. We know not how to advise others for the best, nor how to act ourselves, because that which we apprehend likely to be for our welfare may become a trap. (3.) That therefore our life upon earth is what we have no reason to take any great complacency in, or to be confident of the continuance of. It is to be reckoned by <hi type="italic">days;</hi> it is but a <hi type="italic">vain life,</hi> and we spend it <hi type="italic">as a shadow,</hi> so little is there in it substantial, so fleeting, so uncertain, so transitory is it, and so little in it to be fond of or to be depended on. If all the comforts of life be vanity, life itself can have no great reality in it to constitute a happiness for us. (4.) That our expectations from this world are as uncertain and deceitful as our enjoyments are. Since every thing is vanity, <hi type="italic">Who can tell a man what shall be after him under the sun?</hi> He can no more please himself with the hopes of <hi type="italic">what shall be after him,</hi> to his children and family, than with the relish of what is with him, since he can neither foresee himself, nor can any one else foretel to him, <hi type="italic">what shall be after him.</hi> Nor shall he have any intelligence sent him of it when he is gone. <hi type="italic">His sons come to honour, and he knows it not.</hi> So that, look which way we will, <hi type="italic">Vanity of vanity, all is vanity.</hi>  <chapter eID="Eccl.6"/> <div eID="gen14990" type="x-p"/>

entries.dd09b2dd5b9e10c708b0fb6e18c96e9c04cd9110: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8075"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <div sID="gen12553" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.1-Eccl.6.12">Ec 6:1-12</reference>.<div eID="gen12553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12554" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8075"/><hi type="bold">1. common--</hi>or else more literally,--"great upon man," falls heavily upon man. <div eID="gen12554" type="x-p"/>
entries.dfde652c5bc97b47953d02aabfecaf2f6e5ea9c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8076"/><div sID="gen12555" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8076"/><hi type="bold">2. for his soul--</hi>that is, his enjoyment.<div eID="gen12555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12556" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God giveth him not power to eat--</hi>This distinguishes him from the "rich" man in <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.19">Ec 5:19</reference>. "God hath given" distinguishes him also from the man who got his wealth by "oppression" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.8">Ec 5:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen12556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12557" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stranger--</hi>those not akin, nay, even hostile to him (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.51">Jr 51:51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.5.2">La 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.7.9">Ho 7:9</reference>). He seems to have it in his "power" to do as he will with his wealth, but an unseen power gives him up to his own avarice: God wills that he should toil for "a stranger" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.26">Ec 2:26</reference>), who has found favor in God's sight. <div eID="gen12557" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b3b9596de9538408e5be471415adff2908ccc83: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8077"/><div sID="gen12558" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8077"/>3. Even if a man (of this character) have very many (equivalent to "a hundred," <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.1">2Ki 10:1</reference>) children, and not have a "stranger" as his heir (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.2">Ec 6:2</reference>), and live long ("days of years" express the brevity of life at its best, <reference osisRef="Gen.47.9">Ge 47:9</reference>), yet enjoy no real "good" in life, and lie unhonored, without "burial," at death (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.26">2Ki 9:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.35">35</reference>), the embryo is better than he. In the East to be without burial is the greatest degradation. "Better the fruit that drops from the tree before it is ripe than that left to hang on till rotten" [Henry]. <div eID="gen12558" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6b220eff38171ba2feb67fb4f550a91ea7b0d92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8078"/><div sID="gen12559" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8078"/><hi type="bold">4. he--</hi>rather "it," "the untimely birth." So "its," not "his name."<div eID="gen12559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12560" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with vanity--</hi>to no purpose; a type of the driftless existence of him who makes riches the chief good.<div eID="gen12560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12561" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">darkness--</hi>of the abortive; a type of the unhonored death and dark future beyond the grave of the avaricious. <div eID="gen12561" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0614ceb2ba2082e490a67509f235c55dd57f14c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8079"/><div sID="gen12562" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8079"/><hi type="bold">5. this--</hi>yet "it has more rest than" the toiling, gloomy miser. <div eID="gen12562" type="x-p"/>
entries.34c32f09f401cbcac6be9a16a694005ce90192df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8080"/><div sID="gen12563" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8080"/>6. If the miser's length of "life" be thought to raise him above the abortive, Solomon answers that long life, without enjoying real good, is but lengthened misery, and riches cannot exempt him from going whither "all go." He is fit neither for life, nor death, nor eternity. <div eID="gen12563" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5bbe349163512abffba591e9e199b6d7ca724c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8081"/><div sID="gen12564" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8081"/><hi type="bold">7. man--</hi>rather, "the man," namely, the miser (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.3-Eccl.6.6">Ec 6:3-6</reference>). For not all men labor for the mouth, that is, for selfish gratification.<div eID="gen12564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12565" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appetite--</hi>Hebrew, "the soul." The insatiability of the desire prevents that which is the only end proposed in toils, namely, self-gratification; "the man" thus gets no "good" out of his wealth (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.3">Ec 6:3</reference>). <div eID="gen12565" type="x-p"/>
entries.d836d0da2989d9c623e8e4aa0b177775e7a4caf6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8082"/><div sID="gen12566" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8082"/><hi type="bold">8. For--</hi>"However" [Maurer]. The "for" means (in contrast to the insatiability of the miser), For what else is the advantage which the wise man hath above the fool?"<div eID="gen12566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12567" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">What--</hi>advantage, that is, superiority, above him who knows not how to walk uprightly<div eID="gen12567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12568" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath the poor who knoweth to walk before the living?--</hi>that is, to use and enjoy life aright (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.18">Ec 5:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.19">19</reference>), a cheerful, thankful, godly "walk" (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.9">Psa 116:9</reference>). <div eID="gen12568" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b20516c412a08de8de8fbab6b1223dd03d3a0ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8083"/><div sID="gen12569" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8083"/>9. Answer to the question in <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.8">Ec 6:8</reference>. This is the advantage:<div eID="gen12569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12570" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Better is the sight of the eyes--</hi>the wise man's godly enjoyment of present seen blessings<div eID="gen12570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12571" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">than the (fool's) wandering--</hi>literally, walking (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.9">Psa 73:9</reference>), of the desire, that is, vague, insatiable desires for what he has not (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.7">Ec 6:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.5">He 13:5</reference>).<div eID="gen12571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this--</hi>restless wandering of desire, and not enjoying contentedly the present (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.6">1Ti 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.8">8</reference>). <div eID="gen12572" type="x-p"/>
entries.827f6a25284c97c40f5b9ba49943c3c51bfe459a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8084"/><div sID="gen12573" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8084"/>10. Part II begins here. Since man's toils are vain, what is the chief good? (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.12">Ec 6:12</reference>). The answer is contained in the rest of the book.<div eID="gen12573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12574" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">That which hath been--</hi>man's various circumstances<div eID="gen12574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12575" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is named already--</hi>not only has existed, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.9">Ec 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.15">3:15</reference>, but has received its just name, "vanity," long ago,<div eID="gen12575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12576" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and it is known that it--</hi>vanity<div eID="gen12576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12577" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is man--</hi>Hebrew, "Adam," equivalent to man "of red dust," as his Creator appropriately named him from his frailty.<div eID="gen12577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12578" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither may he contend, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.9.20">Ro 9:20</reference>). <div eID="gen12578" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b42210ada7e4335c510245a8ef18a2515fafbea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8085"/><div sID="gen12579" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8085"/>11. "Seeing" that man cannot escape from the "vanity," which by God's "mighty" will is inherent in earthly things, and cannot call in question God's wisdom in these dispensations (equivalent to "contend," &c.),<div eID="gen12579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12580" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what is man the better--</hi>of these vain things as regards the chief good? None whatever. <div eID="gen12580" type="x-p"/>
entries.1519845f1e6a8fa466b1d3d84114c09c314923fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8086"/><div sID="gen12581" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8086"/><hi type="bold">12. For who knoweth, &c.--</hi>The ungodly know not what is really "good" during life, nor "what shall be after them," that is, what will be the event of their undertakings (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">Ec 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.7">8:7</reference>). The godly might be tempted to "contend with God" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.10">Ec 6:10</reference>) as to His dispensations; but they cannot fully know the wise purposes served by them now and hereafter. Their sufferings from the oppressors are more really good for them than cloudless prosperity; sinners are being allowed to fill up their measure of guilt. Retribution in part vindicates God's ways even now. The judgment shall make all clear. In <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1-Eccl.7.29">Ec 7:1-29</reference>, he states what is good, in answer to this verse. <chapter eID="Eccl.6"/>

entries.f14d7314774cc136059ade490431ddb506de1cc2: <div eID="gen25492" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen25493" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25494" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25494" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25493" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25495" type="x-p"/> The vanity of riches without use, <reference osisRef="Ecc.6.1">Ecc 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.6.2">Ecc 6:2</reference>. Of children and of old age without riches and enjoyment, <reference osisRef="Ecc.6.3-Ecc.6.7">Ecc 6:3-7</reference>. Man does not know what is good for himself, <reference osisRef="Ecc.6.8-Ecc.6.12">Ecc 6:8-12</reference>.
entries.b1fe3b8c6c50c60708ec616b4b363332c1021fe9: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen25495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25496" type="x-p"/> A man to whom God hath given riches - A man may possess much earthly goods, and yet enjoy nothing of them. Possession and fruition are not necessarily joined together; and this is also among the vanities of life. It is worthy of remark, that it belongs to God as much to give the power to enjoy as it does to give the earthly blessings. A wise heathen saw this: - <div eID="gen25496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25497" type="x-p"/> Di tibi divitias dederant, artemque fruendi. <div eID="gen25497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25498" type="x-p"/> Hor. Ep. lib. i., ep. 4, ver. 7. "The gods had given thee riches, and the art to enjoy them."
entries.7ff2bb25e19e4f689a5de5e65e453261edfc6a85: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen25498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25499" type="x-p"/> If a man beget a hundred children - If he have the most numerous family and the largest possessions, and is so much attached to his riches that he grudges himself a monument; an abortion in the eye of reason is to be preferred to such a man; himself is contemptible, and his life worthless. The abortion comes in with vanity - baulks expectation, departs in darkness - never opened its eyes upon the light, and its name is covered with darkness - it has no place in the family register, or in the chronicles of Israel. This, that hath neither seen the sun, nor known any thing is preferable to the miser who has his coffers and granaries well furnished, should he have lived a thousand years, and had a hundred children. He has seen - possessed, no good; and he and the abortion go to one place, equally unknown, and wholly forgotten.
entries.f145e091419d08a8bf8ad104b554520f97af0994: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen25499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25500" type="x-p"/> All the labor of man - This is the grand primary object of all human labor; merely to provide for the support of life by procuring things necessary. And life only exists for the sake of the soul; because man puts these things in place of spiritual good, the appetite - the intense desire after the supreme good - is not satisfied. When man learns to provide as distinctly for his soul as he does for his body, then he will begin to be happy, and may soon attain his end.
entries.8b2bc915c402930b9bf84023825239c984391935: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen25500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25501" type="x-p"/> For what hath the wise more than the fool? - They must both labor for the same end. Both depend upon the labor of themselves or others for the necessaries of life. Both must eat and drink in order to live; and the rich man can no more eat two meals at a time, than he can comfortably wear two changes of raiment. The necessaries of life are the same to both, and their condition in life is nearly similar; liable to the same diseases, dissolution, and death.
entries.87c50c19c547fbaea1e9af3639f2d4cd55c50e05: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen25501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25502" type="x-p"/> Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire - This is translated by the Vulgate, as a sort of adage: Melius est videre quod cupias, quam desiderare quod nescias, "It is better to see what one desires than to covet what one knows not." It is better to enjoy the present than to feed one's self with vain desires of the future. What we translate the wandering of desire, מהלך נפש mehaloch nephesh, is the travelling of the soul. What is this? Does it simply mean desire? Or is there any reference here to the state of separate spirits! It however shows the soul to be in a restless state, and consequently to be unhappy. If Christ dwell in the heart by faith, the soul is then at rest, and this is properly the rest of the people of God.
entries.4e33a7c3594dc8ab70c5d6c2de41ab1b1af379d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen25502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25503" type="x-p"/> That which hath been is named already - The Hebrew of this verse might be translated, "Who is he who is? His name has been already called. And it is known that he is Adam; and that he cannot contend in judgment with him who is stronger than he." "What is more excellent than man; yet can he not, in the lawe, get the victory of him that is mightier than he." - Coverdale. <div eID="gen25503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25504" type="x-p"/> Adam is his name; and it at once points out, <div eID="gen25504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25505" type="x-p"/> 1. His dignity; he was made in the image of God. <div eID="gen25505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25506" type="x-p"/> 2. His fall; he sinned against his Maker and was cast out of Paradise. And <div eID="gen25506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25507" type="x-p"/> 3. His recovery by Christ; the second man (Adam) was the Lord from heaven, and a quickening Spirit.
entries.774e9669bbb299636d36fea01fec24722c0379c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen25507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25508" type="x-p"/> For who knoweth what is good for man in this life - Those things which we deem good are often evil. And those which we think evil are often good. So ignorant are we, that we run the greatest hazard in making a choice. It is better to leave ourselves and our concerns in the hands of the Lord, than to keep them in our own. <div eID="gen25508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25509" type="x-p"/> For who can tell a man what shall be after him - Futurity is with God. While he lives, man wishes to know what is before him. When he is about to die, he wishes to know what will be after him. All this is vanity; God, because he is merciful, will reveal neither.  <chapter eID="Eccl.6"/> <div eID="gen25509" type="x-p"/>

entries.93423db870c5d814d2143b6f83d56500cffbdafc: <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.1">Ecc 6:1</reference> “There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and in great weight it lies upon man: a man to whom God giveth riches, and treasures, and honour, and he wanteth nothing for his soul of all that he may wish, but God giveth him not power to have enjoyment of it, for a strange man hath the enjoyment: that is vanity and an evil disease.” The author presents the result of personal observation; but inasmuch as he relates it in the second tense, he generalizes the matter, and places it scenically before the eyes of the reader. A similar introduction with ישׁ, but without the unnecessary <hi type="italic">asher</hi>, is found at <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.12">Ecc 5:12</reference>; Ecc 10:5. Regarding בּה, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.6">Ecc 8:6</reference>; על does not denote the subj., as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.17">Ecc 2:17</reference> : it appears great to a man, but it has its nearest lying local meaning; it is a great (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.21">Ecc 2:21</reference>) evil, pressing in its greatness heavily upon man. The evil is not the man himself, but the condition in which he is placed, as when, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, the kingdom of heaven is compared to a merchant (Mat 13:45.), - not the merchant in himself, but his conduct and life is a figure of the kingdom of heaven.
entries.1e82d9ad8828e58c8e56d7962a8d0912425bf473: <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.2">Ecc 6:2</reference> <div eID="gen12294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12295" type="x-p"/> To עשׁר וּנך, as at <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.11">2Ch 1:11</reference>, וך and honour is added as a third thing. What follows we do not translate: “and there is nothing wanting ... ;” for that איננּוּ with the pleonastic suff. may mean: “there is not,” is not to be proved from <reference osisRef="Gen.39.9">Gen 39:9</reference>, thus: and he spares not for his soul (lxx καὶ οὐκ κ.τ.λ) what he always desires. חסר is adj. in the sense of wanting, lacking, as at <reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1-1Sam.15.16">1Sa 21:1-15 :16</reference>; 1Ki 11:22; Pro 12:9. לנפשׁו, “for his soul,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, his person, is = the synon. לעצמו found in the later usage of the language; מן (different from the <hi type="italic">min</hi>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.8">Ecc 4:8</reference>) is, as at <reference osisRef="Gen.6.2">Gen 6:2</reference>, partitive. The נכרי, to whom this considerable estate, satisfying every wish, finally comes, is certainly not the legal heir (for that he enters into possession, in spite of the uncertainty of his moral character, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.19">Ecc 2:19</reference>, would be in itself nothing less than a misfortune, yet perfectly in order, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.13">Ecc 5:13</reference> [14]), but some stranger without any just claim, not directly a foreigner (Heiligst.), but, as Burger explains: <hi type="italic">talis qui proprie nullum habet jus in bona ejus cui</hi> נכרי <hi type="italic">dicitur</hi> (cf. נכריּה of the unmarried wife in the Book of Proverbs). <div eID="gen12295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12296" type="x-p"/> That wealth without enjoyment is nothing but vanity and an evil disease, the author now shows by introducing another historical figure, and thereby showing that life without enjoyment is worse than never to have come into existence at all:
entries.5855dfda740b249599ca250b8b0fa93e8959bb3f: <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.3">Ecc 6:3</reference> “If a man begat an hundred, and lived many years, and the amount of the days of his years was great, and his soul satisfied not itself in good, and also he had no grave, then I say: Better than he is the untimely birth.” The accentuation of 3 <hi type="italic">a</hi> is like that of 2 <hi type="italic">a</hi>. The disjunctives follow the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>, as at 2Ki 23:13, only that there Telisha Gedhola stands for Pazer. Hitzig finds difficulty with the clause לו ... וגם־, and regards it as a marginal gloss to 5 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, taken up into the text at a wrong place. But just the unexpected form and the accidental nature, more than the inward necessity of this feature in the figure, leads us to conclude that the author here connects together historical facts, as conjecturally noted above, into one fanciful picture. מאה is obviously to be supplemented by (ובנות) בנים; the Targ. and Midrash make this man to be Cain, Ahab, Haman, and show at least in this that they extend down into the time of the Persian kingdom a spark of historical intelligence. שׁן רבּ interchanges with שׁן הר, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.8">Ecc 11:8</reference>, as at Neh 11:30. In order to designate the long life emphatically, the author expresses the years particularly in days: “and if it is much which (Heiligst.: <hi type="italic">multum est quod</hi>) the days of his years amount to;” cf. ימי ויּהיוּ, in Gen 5. With venaphsho there follows the reverse side of this long life with many children: (1) his soul satisfies not itself, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, has no self-satisfying enjoyment of the good (<hi type="italic">min</hi>, as at <reference osisRef="Ps.104.13">Psa 104:13</reference>, etc.), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of all the good things which he possesses, - in a word, he is not happy in his life; and (2) an honourable burial is not granted to him, but קב חם, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.19">Jer 22:19</reference>, which is the contrary of a burial such as becomes a man (the body of Artaxerxes Ochus was thrown to the cats); whereupon Elster rightly remarks that in an honourable burial and an honourable remembrance, good fortune, albeit shaded with sadness, might be seen. But when now, to one so rich in children and so long-lived, neither enjoyment of his good fortune nor even this shaded glory of an honourable burial is allowed, the author cannot otherwise judge than that the untimely birth is better than he. In this section regarding the uncertainty of riches, we have already, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.14">Ecc 5:14</reference>, fallen on a reminiscence from the Book of Job; it is so much the more probable that here also <reference osisRef="Job.3.16">Job 3:16</reference> has an influence on the formation of the thought. נפל is the foetus which comes lifeless from the mother’s womb.
entries.f0fca1fd39fa1510ae963277bdf6d50af8295eed: <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.4-Eccl.6.5">Ecc 6:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen12296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12297" type="x-p"/> The comparison of an untimely birth with such a man is in favour of the former: “For it cometh in nothingness and departeth in darkness; and with darkness its name is covered. Moreover, it hath not seen the sun, and hath not known: it is better with it than with that other.” It has entered into existence, בּהבל, because it was a lifeless existence into which it entered when its independent life should have begun; and בּהשׁך, it departeth, for it is carried away in all quietness, without noise or ceremony, and “with darkness” its name is covered, for it receives no name and remains a nameless existence, and is forgotten as if it had never been. Not having entered into a living existence, it is also (<hi type="italic">gam</hi>) thus happy to have neither seen the sun nor known and named it, and thus it is spared the sight and the knowledge of all the vanities and evils, the deceptions and sorrows, that are under the sun. When we compare its fate with the long joyless life of that man, the conclusion is apparent: מ ... נחת, plus <hi type="italic">quietis est huic quam illi</hi>, which, with the generalization of the idea of rest (<reference osisRef="Job.3.13">Job 3:13</reference>) in a wider sense, is = <hi type="italic">melius est huic quam illi</hi> (זה ... זה, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.19">Ecc 3:19</reference>). The generalization of the idea proceeds yet further in the Mishn. נוח לו, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>: “It is better (נוח לו לאדם) for a man that he throw himself into a lime-kiln than that (ואל), etc.” From this usage Symm. renders מ ... נחת as obj. to ידע לא, and translates: οὐδὲ ἐπειράθη διαφορᾶς ἑτέρου πράγματος πρὸς ἓτερον ; and Jerome: <hi type="italic">neque cognovit distantiam boni et mali</hi>, - a rendering which is to be rejected, because thus the point of the comparison in which it terminates is broken, for 5 <hi type="italic">b</hi> draws the facit. It is true that this contains a thought to which it is not easy to reconcile oneself. For supposing that life were not in itself, as over against non-existence, a good, there is yet scarcely any life that is absolutely joyless; and a man who has become the father of an hundred children, has, as it appears, sought the enjoyment of life principally in sexual love, and then also has found it richly. But also, if we consider his life less as relating to sense: his children, though not all, yet partly, will have been a joy to him; and has a family life, so lengthened and rich in blessings, only thorns, and no roses at all? And, moreover, how can anything be said of the rest of an untimely birth, which has been without motion and without life, as of a rest excelling the termination of the life of him who has lived long, since rest without a subjective reflection, a rest not felt, certainly does not fall under the point of view of more or less, good or evil? The saying of the author on no side bears the probe of exact thinking. In the main he designs to say: Better, certainly, is no life than a joyless life, and, moreover, one ending dishonourably. And this is only a speciality of the general clause, Ecc 4:2., that death is better than life, and not being born is better than both. The author misunderstands the fact that the earthly life has its chief end beyond itself; and his false eudaemonism, failing to penetrate to the inward fountain of true happiness, which is independent of the outward lot, makes exaggerated and ungrateful demands on the earthly life.
entries.430437980483051ff64daaabb9c587157e2a2e1b: <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.6">Ecc 6:6</reference> <div eID="gen12297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12298" type="x-p"/> A life extending to more than even a thousand years without enjoyment appears to him worthless: “And if he has lived twice a thousand years long, and not seen good - Do not all go hence to one place?” This long period of life, as well as the shortest, sinks into the night of Sheol, and has advantage over the shortest if it wants the ראות ט, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the enjoyment of that which can make man happy. That would be correct if “good” were understood inwardly, ethically, spiritually; but although, according to Koheleth’s view, the fear of God presides over the enjoyment of life, regulating and hallowing it, yet it remains unknown to him that life deepened into fellowship with God is in itself a most real and blessed, and thus the highest good. Regarding אלּוּ (here, as at <reference osisRef="Esth.7.4">Est 7:4</reference>, with perf. foll.: <hi type="italic">etsi vixisset, tamen interrogarem: nonne,</hi> etc.); it occurs also in the oldest liturgical <hi type="italic">Tefilla</hi>, as well as in the prayer <hi type="italic">Nishmath</hi> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Baer’s Siddur, <hi type="italic">Abodath Jisrael</hi>, p. 207). פּ ... אלף, a thousand years twice, and thus an Adam’s life once and yet again. Otherwise Aben Ezra: 1000 years multiplied by itself, thus a million, like פּעמים עשׂרים, 20 x 20 = 400; cf. Targ. <reference osisRef="Isa.30.26">Isa 30:26</reference>, which translates שׁבעתים by 343 = 7 x 7 x 7. Perhaps that is right; for why was not the expression שׁנה אלפּים directly used? The “one place” is, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.20">Ecc 3:20</reference>, the grave and Hades, into which all the living fall. A life extending even to a million of years is worthless, for it terminates at last in nothing. Life has only as much value as it yields of enjoyment.
entries.ceacac91fe5a77edd798b68e90506efcbc1a946c: <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.7">Ecc 6:7</reference> “All the labour of man is for his mouth, and yet his soul has never enough;” or, properly, it is not filled, so that it desires nothing further and nothing more; נמלא used as appropriately of the soul as of the ear, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.8">Ecc 1:8</reference>; for that the mouth and the soul are here placed opposite to one another as “organs of the purely sensual and therefore transitory enjoyment, and of the deeper and more spiritual and therefore more lasting kind of joys” (Zöck.), is an assertion which brings out of the text what it wishes to be in it, - נפשׁ and פּה stand here so little in contrast, that, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.16.26">Pro 16:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.14">Isa 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.8">Isa 29:8</reference>, instead of the soul the stomach could also be named; for it is the soul longing, and that after the means from without of self-preservation, that is here meant; נפשׁ היפה, “beautiful soul,” <hi type="italic">Chullin</hi> iv. 7, is an appetite which is not fastidious, but is contented. גּמו, καὶ ὃμως ὃμως δέ, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.13">Ecc 3:13</reference>; Psa 129:2. All labour, the author means to say, is in the service of the impulse after self-preservation; and yet, although it concentrates all its efforts after this end, it does not bring full satisfaction to the longing soul. This is grounded in the fact that, however in other respects most unlike, men are the same in their unsatisfied longing.
entries.cc2e91be077fc94d9c04d405398e4da6738a3b59: <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.8">Ecc 6:8</reference> “For what hath the wise more than the fool; what the poor who knoweth to walk before the living?” The old translators present nothing for the interpretation, but defend the traditional text; for Jerome, like the Syr., which translates freely, follows the Midrash (fixed in the Targ.), which understands החיים, contrary to the spirit of the book, of the blessed future. The question would be easier if we could, with Bernst. and Ginsburg, introduce a comparat. <hi type="italic">min</hi> before יודע; we would then require to understand by him who knows to walk before the living, some one who acts a part in public life; but how strange a designation of distinguished persons would that be! Thus, as the text stands, יודע ,sdnat is attrib. to לעני, what preference hath the poor, such an one, viz., as understands (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding יודע instead of היודע, under <reference osisRef="Ps.143.10">Psa 143:10</reference>); not: who is intelligent (Aben Ezra); יודע is not, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.11">Ecc 9:11</reference>, an idea contained in itself, but by the foll. הח ... לה (cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.13">Ecc 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.14">Ecc 4:14</reference>; and the <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. form, <reference osisRef="Exod.3.19">Exo 3:19</reference>; Num 22:13; <reference osisRef="Job.34.23">Job 34:23</reference>) obtains the supplement and colouring required: the sequence of the accents (<hi type="italic">Zakeph</hi>, <hi type="italic">Tifcha</hi>, <hi type="italic">Silluk</hi>, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Gen.7.4">Gen 7:4</reference>) is not against this. How the lxx understood its πορευθῆναι κατέναντι τῆς ζωῆς, and the Venet. it’s ἀπιέναι ἀντικρὺ τῆς ζωῆς, is not clear; scarcely as Grätz, with Mendelss.: who, to go against (נגד, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.12">Ecc 4:12</reference>) life, to fight against it, has to exercise himself in self-denial and patience; for “to fight with life” is an expression of modern coinage. הח signifies here, without doubt, not life, but the living. But we explain now, not as Ewald, who separates יודע from the foll. <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. להלך: What profit has then the wise man, the intelligent, patient man, above the fool, that he walks before the living? - by which is meant (but how does this interrog. form agree thereto?), that the wise, patient man has thereby an advantage which makes life endurable by him, in this, that he does not suffer destroying eagerness of desire so to rule over him, but is satisfied to live in quietness.Also this meaning of a quiet life does not lie in the words הח ... הלך. “To know to walk before the living” is, as is now generally acknowledged = to understand the right rule of life (Elst.), to possess the <hi type="italic">savoir vivre</hi> (Heiligst.), to be experienced in the right art of living. the question accordingly is: What advantage has the wise above the fool; and what the poor, who, although poor, yet knows how to maintain his social position? The matter treated of is the insatiable nature of sensual desire. The wise seeks to control his desire; and he who is more closely designated poor, knows how to conceal it; for he lays upon himself restraints, that he may be able to appear and make something of himself. But desire is present in both; and they have in this nothing above the fool, who follows the bent of his desire and lives for the day. He is a fool because he acts as one not free, and without consideration; but, in itself, it is and remains true, that enjoyment and satisfaction stand higher than striving and longing for a thing.
entries.12c202c69e9ce611428d46c512efc966812856b8: <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.9">Ecc 6:9</reference> “Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the soul: also this is vain and windy effort.” We see from the fin. הל־ן interchanging with מר that the latter is not meant of the object (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Ecc 11:9</reference>), but of the action, viz., the “rejoicing in that which one has” (Targ.); but this does not signify <hi type="italic">grassatio</hi>,-<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, <hi type="italic">impetus animae appetentis</hi>, ὁρμὴ τῆς ψυχῆς (cf. <hi type="italic">Marcus Aurelius</hi>, iii. 16), which Knobel, Heiligst., and Ginsburg compare (for הלך means grassari only with certain subjects, as fire, contagion, and the life; and in certain forms, as יהלך for ילך, to which הלך = לכת does not belong), - but <hi type="italic">erratio</hi>, a going out in extent, roving to a distance (cf. הלך, wanderer), ῥεμβασμὸς ἐπιθυμίας, Wisd. 4:12. - Going is the contrast of rest; the soul which does not become full or satisfied goes out, and seeks and reaches not its aim. This insatiableness, characteristic of the soul, this endless unrest, belongs also to the miseries of this present life; for to have and to enjoy is better than this constant <hi type="italic">Hungern und Lungern</hi> hungering and longing. More must not be put into 9 <hi type="italic">a</hi> than already lies in it, as Elster does: “the only enduring enjoyment of life consists in the quiet contemplation of that which, as pleasant and beautiful, it affords, without this mental joy mingling with the desire for the possession of sensual enjoyment.” The conception of “the sight of the eyes” is certainly very beautifully idealized, but in opposition to the text. If 9 <hi type="italic">a</hi> must be a moral proverb, then Luther’s rendering is the best: “It is better to enjoy the present good, than to think about other good.”
entries.755d19729858d67cf94a7881e89b598f379f0e1b: <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.10">Ecc 6:10</reference> “That which hath been, its name hath long ago been named; and it is determined what a man shall be: and he cannot dispute with Him who is stronger than he.” According to the usage of the tense, it would be more correct to translate: That which (at any time) has made its appearance, the name of which was long ago named, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of which the <hi type="italic">What?</hi> and the <hi type="italic">How?</hi> were long ago determined, and, so to speak, formulated. This שׁ ... כּבר does not stand parallel to היה כבר, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.10">Ecc 1:10</reference>; for the expression here does not refer to the sphere of that which is done, but of the predetermination. Accordingly, אדם ... ונו is also to be understood. Against the accents, inconsistently periodizing and losing sight of the comprehensiveness of אדם ... אשׁר, Hitzig renders: “and it is known that, if one is a man, he cannot contend,” etc., which is impossible for this reason, that אדם הוא cannot be a conditional clause enclosed within the sentence יוכל ... אשׁר. Obviously ונודע, which in the sense of <hi type="italic">constat</hi> would be a useless waste of words, stands parallel to שׁמו נקרא, and signifies known, viz., previously known, as passive of ידע, in the sense of Zec 14:7; cf. Psa 139:1. Bullock rightly compares Act 15:18. After ידע, <hi type="italic">asher</hi>, like <hi type="italic">ki</hi>, which is more common, may signify “that,” <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.12">Ecc 8:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.26">Eze 20:26</reference>; but neither “that he is a man” (Knobel, Vaih., Luzz., Hengst., Ginsb.), nor “that he is the man” (Ewald, Elst., Zöckler), affords a consistent meaning. As mah after yada' means <hi type="italic">quid</hi>, so <hi type="italic">asher</hi> after it may mean <hi type="italic">quod</hi> = that which (cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.8.19">Dan 8:19</reference>, although it does not at all stand in need of proof); and <hi type="italic">id quod homo est</hi> (we cannot render הוּא without the expression of a definite conception of time) is intended to mean that the whole being of a man, whether of this one or that one, at all times and on all sides, is previously known; cf. to this pregnant substantival sentence, Ecc 12:13. Against this formation of his nature and of his fate by a higher hand, man cannot utter a word. <div eID="gen12298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12299" type="x-p"/> The thought in 10b is the same as that at <reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">Isa 45:9</reference>; Rom 9:20. The Chethı̂b שׁהתּקּיף<note placement="foot">With <hi type="italic">He</hi> unpointed, because it is omitted in the Kerı̂, as in like manner in כּשׁה, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.3">Ecc 10:3</reference>, שׁה, Lam 5:18. In the bibl. Rabb., the ה is noted as superfluous.</note> is not inadmissible, for the stronger than man is מנּהּ ... מרי. Also התקיף might in any case be read: with one who overcomes him, has and manifests the ascendency over him. There is indeed no <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הת .hpiH  found in the language of the Bible (Herzf. and Fürst compare הג, <reference osisRef="Ps.12.5">Psa 12:5</reference>); but in the Targ., אתקף is common; and in the school-language of the Talm., הת is used of the raising of weighty objections, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <hi type="italic">Kamma</hi> 71 <hi type="italic">a</hi>. The verb, however, especially in the perf., is in the passage before us less appropriate. In לא־יוּכל lie together the ideas of physical (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.43.32">Gen 43:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.12.17">Deu 12:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.16.5">Deu 16:5</reference>, etc.) and moral inability.
entries.554c37cbd4bfc20ac9be657a5c7d4c377f36bed0: <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.11">Ecc 6:11</reference> “For there are many words which increase vanity: What cometh forth therefrom for man?” The dispute (objection), דּין, takes place in words; דּברים here will thus not mean “things” (Hengst., Ginsb., Zöckl., Bullock, etc.), but “words.” As that wrestling or contending against God’s decision and providence is vain and worthless, nothing else remains for man but to be submissive, and to acknowledge his limitation by the fear of God; thus there are also many words which only increase yet more the multitude of vanities already existing in this world, for, because they are resultless, they bring no advantage for man. Rightly, Elster finds herein a hint pointing to the influence of the learning of the Jewish schools already existing in <hi type="italic">Koheleth</hi>'s time. We know from Josephus that the problem of human freedom and of God’s absoluteness was a point of controversy between opposing parties: the Sadducees so emphasized human freedom, that they not only excluded (<hi type="italic">Antt.</hi> xiii. 5. 9; <hi type="italic">Bell</hi>. ii. 8. 14) all divine predetermination, but also co-operation; the Pharisees, on the contrary supposed an interconnection between divine predetermination (εἱμαρμένη) and human freedom (<hi type="italic">Antt.</hi> xiii. 5. 9, xviii. 1. 3; <hi type="italic">Bell</hi>. ii. 8. 14). The Talm. affords us a glance at this controversy; but the statement in the Talm. (in <hi type="italic">Berachoth</hi> 33 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, and elsewhere), which conditions all by the power of God manifesting itself in history, but defends the freedom of the religious-moral self-determination of man, may be regarded as a Pharisaic maxim. In Rom 9, Paul places himself on this side; and the author of the Book of Koheleth would subscribe this passage as his testimony, for the “fear God” is the “<hi type="italic">kern und stern</hi>” kernel and star of his pessimistic book.
entries.d057a97360ca0666896d47dbc103f3f489e5a6d2: <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.12">Ecc 6:12</reference> <div eID="gen12299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12300" type="x-p"/> Man ought to fear God, and also, without dispute and murmuring, submit to His sway: “For who knoweth what is good for man in life during the number of the days of his vain life, and which he spendeth like a shadow? No one can certainly show a man what shall be after him under the sun.” We translate אשׁר only by “<hi type="italic">ja</hi>” (“certainly”), because in Germ. no interrogative can follow “<hi type="italic">dieweil</hi>” (“because”). The clause with asher (as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.9">Ecc 4:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11">Ecc 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.15">Ecc 10:15</reference>; cf. Song, under Sol 5:2), according to its meaning not different from <hi type="italic">ki</hi>, is related in the way of proof to that beginning with <hi type="italic">ki</hi>. Man is placed in our presence. To be able to say to him what is good for him, - <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, what position he must take in life, what direction he must give to his activity, what decision he must adopt in difficult and important cases, - we ought not only to be able to penetrate his future, but, generally, the future; but, as <hi type="italic">Tropfen</hi> drops in the stream of history, we are poor <hi type="italic">Tröpfe</hi> simpletons, who are hedged up within the present. Regarding the accus. of duration, וגו מספּר, pointing to the brevity of human life, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Ecc 2:3. With הבלו, the attribute of breath-like transitiveness is assigned to life (as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ecc 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.9">Ecc 9:9</reference>) (as already in the name given to Abel, the second son of Adam), which is continued by כּ ויע with the force of a relative clause, which is frequently the case after preceding part. attrib., <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Isa 5:23. We translate: which he spendeth like the (1) shadow [in the nom.] (after <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.13">Ecc 8:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.14.2">Job 14:2</reference>); not: like a shadow [in the accus.]; for although the days of life are also likened to a shadow, <reference osisRef="Ps.144.4">Psa 144:4</reference>, etc., yet this use of עשׂה does not accord therewith, which, without being a Graecism (Zirkel, Grätz), harmonises with the Greek phrase, ποιεῖν χρόνον, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.33">Act 15:33</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.13.23">Pro 13:23</reference>, lxx (also with the Lat. <hi type="italic">facere dies</hi> of Cicero, etc.). Thus also in the Syr. and Palest.-Aram. lacad is used of time, in the sense of <hi type="italic">transigere</hi>. Aharav does not mean: after his present condition (Zöckl.); but, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">Ecc 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.14">Ecc 7:14</reference> : after he has passed away from this scene. Luzz. explains it correctly: Whether his children will remain in life? Whether the wealth he has wearied himself in acquiring will remain and be useful to them? But these are only illustrations. The author means to say, that a man can say, neither to himself nor to another, what in definite cases is the real advantage; because, in order to say this, he must be able to look far into the future beyond the limits of the individual life of man, which is only a small member of a great whole.  <chapter eID="Eccl.6"/> <div eID="gen12300" type="x-p"/>

Or rather 2. the Abortive; of whom alone, and not of the former, that passage is true, <ns0:hi>He hath not seen the Sun,</ns0:hi> v. 5</ns0:note> cometh in <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Into the World, this word being oft put for a Man's being Born, as <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 1. 21. <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 5. 15.</ns0:note> with vanity <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>in vain,</ns0:hi> to no purpose; without any comfort or benefit by it, which also is in a great measure the case of the covetous wretch.</ns0:note>, and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />parteth in darkness <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Dieth obscurely without any Obser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vation or regard of men.</ns0:note>, and his name shall be covered with darkness <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Shall be speedily and utterly forgot<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ten, whereas the Name of such wicked men shall rot, and be remembred to their shame.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Moreover, he hath not seen the sun <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">He never beheld the light, and therefore it is not grievous to him to want it, whereas the covetous Man saw that light was very pleasant, and therefore the loss of it was irksom to him.</ns0:note>, nor known <ns0:hi>any thing</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Hath had no knowledge, sense or experience of any thing whether good or evil.</ns0:note>: this <ns0:hi>hath</ns0:hi> more rest <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Because he is perfectly free from all those incumbran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces and vexations to which the covetous Man is long exposed.</ns0:note> than the other.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 Yea, though he live a thousand years twice <ns0:hi>told</ns0:hi>

And so after a little time all are alike as to this life, of which he here speaks, and as to the other life his condition is infi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nitely worse than that of an untimely birth.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Pro. 16. 26.</ns0:note> All the labour of man <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> for his mouth <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">For Meat to put into his Mouth, that he may get food; and a Bread is oft put for all food, so food is put for all necessary Provi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sions for this life, as <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 30. 8. and elsewhere, whereof this is the chief, for which a Man will sell his House and Lands, yea the very Garments upon his back.</ns0:note>, and yet the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Soul.</ns0:note> appetite is not filled <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Although all that a Man can get by his labours is but necessary f<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>od, which the meanest sort of men commonly enjoy, as is observed in the next Verse, yet such is the vanity of this World and the folly of Mankind, that men are in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />satiable in their desires, and restless in their endeavours, after more and more, and never say, they have enough.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 For what hath the wise more than the fool <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">To wit, in these matters. Both are equally subject to the same calamities, and partakers of the same comforts of this Life.</ns0:note>? what hath the poor, that knoweth to walk before the living <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">To wit, before the poor that doth not know this? Which words are easily understood by comparing this clause with the former. And such defects are usual both in Scripture and other Authors, as hath been formerly noted, by a Figure which the Learned call <ns0:hi>Ananta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />podoton.</ns0:hi> And by this Phrase, <ns0:hi>that knoweth,</ns0:hi> &c. he means such a poor Man who is ingenious and industrious, who is fit for service and business, and knows how to carry himself towards rich men, so as to deserve and gain their favour, and to procure a livelihood.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="10">10 That which hath been is named already <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This verse is added either as a proof of what he last said con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning the vanity and wandring of unsatiable desires; or as a fur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther instance of the vanity of all things in this Life. <ns0:hi>That which hath been</ns0:hi> (or <ns0:hi>is,</ns0:hi> for the Hebrew verb may be rendred either way, to wit, Man, considered with all his endowments and enjoyments, whether he be wise or foolish, rich or poor, Man, who is the chief of all visible and sublunary beings, for whom they were all made) <ns0:hi>is named already,</ns0:hi> to wit, by God, who<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> presently after his Creation, gave him the following name, to signifie what his nature and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dition was or would be. Heb. <ns0:hi>What is that which hath been,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>is,</ns0:hi> it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>hath been named already.</ns0:hi> Others understand it thus, All the seve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral conditions which men have had or shall have in the World, Riches or Poverty, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> are already named, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> appointed or de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />termined by Gods unchangeable Counsel, and invincible Provi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence: But though this be true, it seems not to suit so well with the following clause, as the other Interpretation doth.</ns0:note>, and it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> known that it is man <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">This is certain and manifest, that that being, which makes all this noise and stir in the world, howsoever magnified by themselves, and somtimes adored by Flatterers, and howsoever differenced from, or advanced above others, by Wisdom or Riches, or the like, is but a <ns0:hi>Man, i. e.</ns0:hi> a mean, earthly<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> mortal and miserable Creature, as his very name signifies, which God gave him for this very end, that he might be always sensible of his vain, and base, and miserable estate in this world, and therefore never expect satisfaction or hap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />piness in it.</ns0:note>: neither may he contend with him that is mightier than he <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> With Almighty God, with whom Men are ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry apt to contend upon every sleight occasion, and against whom they are ready to murmur for this Vanity, and Mortality, and Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sery of Mankind, although they brought it upon themselves by their own sins. So this is seasonably added to prevent the abuse of the foregoing passage.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Seeing there be many things that increase vanity <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">This seems to be added as a Conclusion of the Disputation ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />naged in all the foregoing Chapters, <ns0:hi>seeing</ns0:hi> not only Man is a vain Creature in himself, as hath been now said, but <ns0:hi>there are</ns0:hi> also <ns0:hi>many</ns0:hi> other <ns0:hi>things</ns0:hi> in the world, <ns0:hi>which</ns0:hi> instead of removing or diminish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, as might be expected, do but <ns0:hi>increase</ns0:hi> this <ns0:hi>vanity,</ns0:hi> as Wisdom, Pleasure, Power, Wealth, and the like, the vanity of all which hath been fully and particularly declared.
